start: Lay the sources out like piles of cards, each sorted with its smallest card on top. The next value out must be one of the top cards, since everything under a top card is at least as big. So take the smallest top card, and turn over a new card only on the pile it came from, and only when someone asks for the next value.

Keep the tops in a min-heap of `(value, i)` pairs, where `i` is the source's position: it breaks ties between equal values and tells you which iterator to advance. Pop the smallest and `yield` it; when the caller asks again, read that source's next value, check it is an `int` no smaller than the one just yielded, and push it. A `yield` in `merge_streams` makes it a generator, so nothing is read before the first `next()`.

start.text: The shape, with the reads and checks left to you. Note where the second read happens: after the `yield`, not before it.
start.code:
import heapq

def merge_streams(streams):
    its = [iter(s) for s in streams]
    heap = []
    for i, it in enumerate(its):
        ...  # read one head (skip an empty source), check it is an int, add (head, i)
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    while heap:
        value, i = heapq.heappop(heap)
        yield value
        ...  # only now read the next value of its[i]: skip if exhausted, check it, push it

test_examples_empty_duplicates: `[[1, 4], [], [1, 3, 8]]` must give `[1, 1, 3, 4, 8]`: the empty source has no head at all, and both 1s are kept, because merging does not remove repeats. `merge_streams([])`, with no sources, must give an empty iterator, not an error.

If this errors on the empty source, your code read its first value without handling the end: a source can be exhausted before it gives anything. Catch `StopIteration` around each read and leave that source out.
test_seeded_oracle: 30 random cases, each with up to 7 sources of up to 9 sorted values between -10 and 10, so empty sources, negatives and repeats are all common. The output must equal every value from every source, sorted together.
Values missing from the end usually mean the whole merge stopped when one source ran out. An exhausted source only leaves the heap; the others carry on until the heap is empty.
test_lazy_consumption: Two generator sources count every value read from them. Straight after `merge_streams(...)` the counts must be `[0, 0]`, so nothing may be read before the first `next()`: a `yield` in the body of `merge_streams` does that. A function that reads the heads and then returns an iterator has already read one value from each.

After the first `next()`, which gives 1, each source has been read once, `[1, 1]`; after the second, which gives 2, it is `[2, 1]`. Reading source 0's next value before handing out its 1 makes the counts `[2, 1]` too early: read after the `yield`.
test_late_invalid_order: `merge_streams([[1, 0]])` must hand out 1, then raise `ValueError` on the second `next()`, when 0 is read and found smaller than the 1 before it. If the first `next()` raises instead, you read the 0 before yielding the 1.

`list(merge_streams([[None]]))` must raise `ValueError` as well, so check the type of every value read, each source's first one included. Using `None` as the default in `next(it, None)` makes `[[None]]` look empty: catch `StopIteration`, or use a fresh `object()` as the default.

TypeError: `'list' object is not an iterator` means `next()` was called on a list. Call `iter()` once on each source, keep those iterators, and call `next()` on them. The lazy test passes generators, so reading by index, `stream[pos]`, fails there too.

`'<' not supported between instances of 'list_iterator' and 'list_iterator'` means the heap compared iterators because two values tied. Store `(value, i)` with the source's position `i`, and look the iterator up by `i`.
RuntimeError: `generator raised StopIteration` means `next()` hit the end of a source inside your generator, and Python turns that into a `RuntimeError`. The empty source `[]` does it on the very first read. Wrap each read in `try`/`except StopIteration` and leave that source out.
ValueError: A `ValueError` from the test's first `next(result)` on `[[1, 0]]` means your code read and checked the 0 before handing out the 1. Yield first, then read the next value from the source you popped.

stopped: `next(iter(streams[i]))` starts a fresh iterator each time, so for a list it returns the first value forever and the heap never empties. Call `iter()` once per source, before the loop, and keep using those iterators.

`list(...)` in the tests keeps asking until your generator stops. If you push the popped value back instead of the source's next value, the same number comes out forever: push only a newly read value, and nothing once the source is exhausted.
passing: All passing. Check the memory claim as your own input: `sum(merge_streams([range(i, 100000, 100) for i in range(100)]))` merges 100 sources of 1,000 values each, and its peak memory should stay near 100 heads, not 100,000 values. Then the README's follow-up: if one source is slow to answer, what may you still emit?
